name: Inspector-General of Police v All Nigeria Peoples Party
summary: A key modern case on public rallies, police permits, and the constitutional freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
facts: Political parties sought to hold rallies. Police reliance on permit/control regimes was challenged as inconsistent with the constitutional right to peaceful assembly.
issues: Whether police permit requirements can extinguish the right to peaceful public assembly.
How section 40 interacts with public-order policing.
holding: The decision is taught for rejecting a regime in which peaceful assembly depends on police permission in a way that undermines section 40. Confirm the exact orders and reasoning in a licensed report.
ratio: The constitutional right to peaceful assembly and association cannot be reduced to a mere privilege dependent on police permission; public-order regulation must remain consistent with section 40.
report_citation: See NWLR / law-report citation via a licensed law-report service

interpretations.body: Use this case when studying protests and political rallies. Distinguish notice/coordination for traffic and safety from a veto power that effectively bans assembly. Cross-link to the Emergencies scenario on joining a protest.
Always check later Public Order Act amendments and subsequent cases. The educational point is constitutional primacy: statutes and police practice must be read subject to Chapter IV.
